title: Felix and the Visitor
premise: Ansel Okonkwo, a late-night radio host, begins receiving calls from listeners who died the previous week, and every photograph from their late grandmother's house now shows an extra chair at the kitchen table. As Ansel investigates, they learn that ten years ago the family 'invited in' a presence to settle an old injustice—one the law never punished—and the entity has come to collect its fee: the last living resident of the house must sign over their memory of the crime. Ansel's sister Ruth, the executor, is being pressured to sign the papers and surrender what she knows about their grandfather's buried wrongdoing. Ansel must hold out until sunrise, choosing between protecting Ruth's love for them and the truth that could free the house's dead, and in the end Ansel signs in Ruth's place, remembering everything at last—and the chair in the photographs is finally occupied, and finally empty.
about_author: Yara Villalobos is a former community-radio producer from the Gulf Coast who writes horror rooted in family archives, inheritance, and the things houses remember. 'Felix and the Visitor' is her second novel, inspired by a box of unlabeled photographs left to her by an aunt.

chapters.title: The Dead Air Slot
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Hosting the 2 a.m. shift, Ansel takes a call from a woman who describes her own funeral from last Tuesday. The emotional beat is professional disbelief curdling into private dread as a second dead caller confirms details only the deceased would know.

chapters.title: Grandma's Kitchen, Twice
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Sorting the estate, Ansel notices every family photograph now includes an extra wooden chair at the kitchen table—photos taken decades apart. Ruth laughs it off. The beat is the first crack in Ansel's ten-year habit of explaining away the impossible.

chapters.title: Caller on the Line
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The dead callers begin asking Ansel questions instead of telling stories: 'Who signed the guest book?' Ansel realizes they're not haunting—they're warning. The beat is the vertigo of realizing the calls are addressed to Ansel personally.

chapters.title: What Ruth Carries
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. As executor, Ruth finds a locked cedar box and a lawyer's letter referencing 'the arrangement of 2014.' She hides both from Ansel. The beat is her protective love curdling into complicity.

chapters.title: The Chair Moves Closer
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. In new photographs taken that week, the chair has moved—closer to the camera, closer to the table's head. Ansel tests the house with a live-streamed photo; the chair appears even on camera. The beat is the collapse of every rational explanation.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Noises
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV, flashback. A chapter of the 'explanations' Ansel built over a decade: pipes, raccoons, the furnace. Interleaved, the night in 2014 the family gathered and 'invited in' something to make an injustice right—memory blurred, deliberately. The beat is grief for one's own edited past.

chapters.title: Felix
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The dead callers begin calling Ansel 'Felix'—a name no one uses, a name from the blurred summer of 2014. Ansel searches old radio archives and finds their own voice on a tape they don't remember recording. The beat is the horror of being a stranger to oneself.

chapters.title: The Papers
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. The lawyer delivers documents: the house transfers to 'the seated party' upon the last resident's signature, and the signer's memory of 2014 is the consideration. Ruth reads the name on the beneficiary line: Felix. The beat is dread sharpening into a moral choice.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Digging into family history, Ansel learns what the law never touched: a death in 1994, ruled accidental, that the family knew was not. The invited presence was hired to do what courts wouldn't. The beat is horrified understanding that the family were both victims and perpetrators.

chapters.title: The Guest Book
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. In the cedar box, Ansel finds the guest book from 2014 with their own signature—inviting the Visitor in, volunteering the family. The chair in the photographs is the guest's seat, and it has been waiting to be sat in. The beat is guilt made physical.

chapters.title: Ruth Decides
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth resolves to sign the papers herself and take the memory, sparing Ansel. She visits the house at dusk and hears the chair scrape toward the table. The beat is sacrificial love meeting an appetite that doesn't distinguish givers.

chapters.title: The Last Broadcast
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. On air, Ansel asks the dead callers directly how to un-invite what was invited. The answer: the invitation can be revoked only by the inviter, at the house, before sunrise, before signing. The beat is fragile hope with a deadline attached.

chapters.title: Locked In
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel reaches the house at midnight to find Ruth already there, pen in hand, doors that were open now closed. The house will not let either leave until someone signs. The beat is claustrophobia and the first open confrontation with the Visitor's presence.

chapters.title: What the Visitor Wants
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The Visitor speaks through the radio in the kitchen: it doesn't want the house—it wants the memory of the crime witnessed, held, owned. A signature is consent to remember forever. The beat is the realization that the horror is a demand for truth.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Trapped together, Ruth finally tells Ansel what she has carried since 2014: that Ansel, as Felix, invited the Visitor to protect her, and paid by having the memory taken. Her hidden love and guilt pour out. The beat is devastating tenderness.

chapters.title: The Signature
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ruth lifts the pen; Ansel takes it from her. Choosing love against duty—duty being silence, love being witness—Ansel signs, and the memory of 2014 floods back whole: the crime, the grief, the invitation, the price. The beat is the climax: reclaiming a stolen self.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV, minutes before dawn. Holding the full memory, Ansel speaks the revocation aloud—but the Visitor shows the cost: the dead callers' voices begin fading, their unfinished business unresolved. The beat is the terrible arithmetic of one truth against many restings.

chapters.title: The Chair, Occupied
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel offers a counter-deal: their memory, freely witnessed, broadcast—Ansel will tell the crime on air, in daylight, to the living, so the dead are heard without the Visitor keeping them. In the final photograph, someone sits in the chair. The beat is courage as negotiation.

chapters.title: The Morning Show
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. At sunrise, on live radio, Ansel names the 1994 crime, the family's cover-up, and their own complicity. Callers who died last week call in one by one to say thank you and goodbye. The beat is catharsis—justice outside the law, delivered by testimony.

chapters.title: Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. The photographs now show the chair empty, pushed back as if a guest has finally left. The house is quiet in a new way. Ruth and Ansel burn the papers unsigned by anyone but Ansel—and find the signature has faded. The beat is exhausted, uncertain relief.

chapters.title: What Ansel Kept
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The Visitor kept one thing as its fee: not the memory of the crime, but the memory of the ten years of explanations—Ansel remembers 2014 but not the decade of denial, a mercy or a wound. The beat is bittersweet reckoning with an imperfect rescue.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Weeks later, Ansel hosts the final 2 a.m. shift; the line is quiet, the dead at rest. On the last family photograph, the chair remains—but at the table's head sits a place setting no one questions, and Ansel, for the first time, sets a cup there too. The beat is peace negotiated with the past, memory held rather than erased.
